summary: Updates the Back-to-Back Frames benchmark procedure of RFC 2544, a classic method for testing network devices, based on experience since it was written. It updates Section 26.4 of RFC 2544.

eli5.summary: A better way to run one old speed test for network equipment, learned by trying it in the real world.

questions: what is the back-to-back frames benchmark
how to measure network device buffer size
what is corrected dut buffer time
subtitle: A refreshed recipe for measuring how long a burst of frames a network device can absorb without loss.

tldr.problem: The Back-to-Back Frames test in RFC 2544 gave results that were hard to repeat, and for some frame sizes it reported buffer times that were clearly wrong, such as 30 seconds.
tldr.mechanism: The update uses the Throughput results to skip frame sizes where no buffering can happen, requires a proven binary search, repeats the test N times with summary statistics, and corrects the buffer estimate for frames the device forwarded during the burst.
tldr.outcome: Testers get a more efficient procedure and a corrected buffer time they can sanity check. It is an Informational memo that updates Section 26.4 of RFC 2544.

today: RFC 9004 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2544, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it. Its method replaces the Back-to-Back Frames procedure of Section 26.4 of RFC 2544.

sections.title: Why RFC 2544 Needed an Update
sections.content:
RFC 2544 defines the IETF's basic benchmarking methods for network interconnect devices. Section 26.4 of that RFC describes the Back-to-Back Frames benchmark. Recent testing experience showed that buffer size matters when software packet processing is interrupted, which makes this benchmark more important than before.

This memo changes only that one test. It uses the requirements words of RFC 8174, and it is meant for people running laboratory tests and for people building devices that support those tests.

Mixtures of frame sizes (IMIX, as in RFC 6985) MUST NOT be used for this test. Buffer testing with several ingress ports overloading one egress port, as in RFC 8239, is a different method, and that RFC SHOULD be used when the egress buffer is the known point of overload.
sections.eli5: An old speed test for network boxes was giving odd answers. This memo fixes the recipe for just that one test.

sections.title: What the Old Test Got Wrong
sections.content:
The test sends a burst of frames at the minimum allowed spacing to see how long a burst the Device Under Test (DUT) can handle without loss. Results from the OPNFV VSPERF continuous integration testing showed that the benchmark was very consistent for some frame sizes and somewhat variable for others.

For large frame sizes the zero-loss burst translated to 30 seconds of buffer time, which was clearly wrong or highly suspect. For some sizes the test cannot exceed the frame-header-processing rate of the DUT, so no buffering occurs and the result reflects the test equipment rather than the DUT.

The memo models the DUT as an ingress, a buffer, a header-processing function with limited speed, and an egress. During a burst, frames arrive at the Max Theoretical Frame Rate while HeaderProc drains the buffer at the Measured Throughput. A raw burst length therefore overstates the buffer, because many frames have already left by the time the burst ends.
sections.eli5: If you pour water into a sink while the drain is open, the sink seems to hold more than it really does. The old test forgot about the drain.

sections.title: The Updated Test Procedure
sections.content:
Before testing, the Throughput benchmark of Section 26.1 of RFC 2544 MUST be available for all recommended frame sizes, measured under zero loss and with the same traffic characteristics as the Back-to-Back test. Only frame sizes whose Measured Throughput was below the Max Theoretical Frame Rate are tested, because only those can overflow the buffers.

Each trial sends a burst after idle time at the minimum interframe gap and counts the frames the DUT forwards. A trial has three required parts: the time to send the burst, the time to receive it at the Throughput rate, and at least 2 seconds not overlapping the receive time so that the DUT buffers deplete. The upper search limit for the burst sending time MUST be configurable to values as high as 30 seconds. A result at or near that limit is likely invalid and the test MUST be repeated with a higher limit.

The search for the longest lossless burst MUST use either the Binary Search or the Binary Search with Loss Verification from ETSI TST009, with the burst length in frames replacing the offered load. The algorithm inputs and the minimum step size MUST be reported.

The test MUST be repeated N times per frame size, where N is now a variable that must be reported. Each repetition is an independent search, and each result is kept for further processing.
sections.eli5: Pick the cases where the sink can really overflow, then keep adding water in bigger and smaller scoops until you find the biggest scoop that never spills. Do it many times and wait for the sink to empty in between.

sections.title: Calculations and Reporting
sections.content:
For each frame size, the tester calculates the average (the benchmark), minimum, maximum and standard deviation of the longest Back-to-Back Frame values over the N tests. It then computes two times in seconds. The Implied DUT Buffer Time is the average burst length divided by the Max Theoretical Frame Rate. The Corrected DUT Buffer Time subtracts the part of that time that the DUT spent forwarding frames during the burst.

Both rates MUST be in frames per second in the equation. If Measured Throughput is not available, the received frame rate during Back-to-Back testing is an acceptable approximation.

Results SHOULD be reported as a table with a row per frame size, with the average frame count, the minimum, maximum and standard deviation, and the Corrected DUT Buffer Time. The number of tests N MUST be reported, along with the minimum search step size. If the tester has a specific frame rate of interest below the Throughput rate, an Actual Buffer Time can also be estimated and reported, properly labeled.
sections.eli5: After many tries you average the results and then subtract the water that already drained away, to get the true size of the sink.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The benchmarking is limited to controlled laboratory stimuli with dedicated address space. The test network MUST NOT be connected to devices that may forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the test management network.

Testing is done on an opaque-box basis, relying only on what can be measured from outside the DUT. The memo warns that DUT developers might have incentives to alter performance when test conditions can be detected, so special capabilities SHOULD NOT exist in the DUT for benchmarking purposes. The procedures here are not designed to detect such activity. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Test only in a closed lab, and do not let the device cheat when it knows it is being tested.

data.title: Buffer time calculations
data.code:
Implied DUT buffer time =
   Average num of Back-to-back Frames / Max Theoretical Frame Rate

Corrected DUT Buffer Time =
   Implied DUT Buffer Time -
   (Implied DUT Buffer Time * Measured Throughput / Max Theoretical Frame Rate)

items.title: Send time
items.text: Time to send the burst at the back-to-back rate, set by the search algorithm.

items.title: Receive time
items.text: Time to receive the burst at the Throughput rate, including DUT latency.

items.title: Depletion time
items.text: At least 2 seconds so the DUT buffers can empty.
